nameStory: The Cylindrical Click Beetle gets its name from two distinctive features: its elongated, tube-like body shape that resembles a tiny cylinder, and its amazing ability to 'click' itself right-side up when flipped over. The clicking sound comes from a special hinge mechanism between body segments that acts like a spring-loaded trap, launching the beetle into the air with an audible snap!
description: The Cylindrical Click Beetle is a small, elongated beetle with a distinctly narrow, tube-shaped body that sets it apart from most other insects. These beetles are typically dark brown to black in color and have a sleek, streamlined appearance. They're part of a large family of beetles famous for their acrobatic clicking ability - if you find one on its back, watch as it arches its body and snaps itself upright with a satisfying click sound. Adults are usually found crawling on or under bark of dead and dying trees.

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Distinctly cylindrical and elongated body, much more narrow and tube-like than most beetles - feels smooth and hard like a tiny wooden dowel when gently handled

idTips.label: Click Mechanism
idTips.description: When placed on its back, arches its body dramatically and snaps upright with an audible 'click' - you can actually feel the vibration if it's in your palm

idTips.label: Color Pattern
idTips.description: Dark brown to blackish coloration with a subtle matte finish, lacking any bright spots or metallic sheen

idTips.label: Antennae
idTips.description: Thread-like antennae that are proportionally long for the body size, often held close to the head when at rest

idTips.label: Surface Texture
idTips.description: Smooth, hard exoskeleton with very fine, barely visible punctures - feels like touching a polished pebble

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Small beetle, typically fitting comfortably on a fingertip with room to spare

habitat: Look for Cylindrical Click Beetles in mature forests with plenty of dead and decaying hardwood trees, especially oak, maple, and birch. They're most commonly found under loose bark, in rotting logs, or crawling on the surface of dead wood where their larvae develop. These beetles prefer moist, shaded woodland environments from sea level to mid-elevation forests throughout New England.

seasonality.spring: Adults become active as temperatures warm, often found under bark or emerging from overwintering sites in rotting logs. This is when mating activity begins.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when adults are most commonly encountered crawling on dead wood surfaces, especially during warm, humid evenings. Females are laying eggs in decaying wood.
seasonality.fall: Adults continue to be active into early fall, preparing for winter by seeking shelter under bark or deep in rotting logs. New generation may be emerging.
seasonality.winter: Adults hibernate deep in rotting logs or under thick bark layers. Larvae continue developing slowly in their wood galleries throughout the cold months.

funFact: Click beetle larvae, called wireworms, can live for several years boring through dead wood - some species take up to 5 years to become adults, making them among the longest-lived beetle larvae in New England forests!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other dark, elongated beetles found in dead wood, but the cylindrical shape and clicking ability are unique. Remember: if it's truly tube-shaped and can launch itself with a click, you've found a click beetle!
contextualKnowledge: While called 'click' beetles, the clicking isn't just for show - it's actually an escape mechanism that startles predators and helps right the beetle when it falls on its back. The family name Elateridae comes from the Greek word 'elater' meaning 'driver' or 'hurler,' referring to this spring-loaded jumping ability.
compareHints: Since this is the only Sylvanelater species in New England, compare it to other click beetles in the region by its distinctly cylindrical body shape - most other click beetles are more flattened or oval. The smooth, matte finish and preference for hardwood forests also help distinguish it from the more common click beetles found in agricultural areas or coniferous forests.
